articles.title: For Brazil’s Indigenous youth, visibility is resistance
articles.summary: As climate change reshapes Indigenous territories across Brazil, a new generation is turning to culture and digital platforms to defend their lands and their future.
articles.content:
They are watching rising temperatures, vanishing food sources, devastating wildfires and the accelerating loss of ancestral territory – but they are also claiming new space online, using social media, music, photography and dance as tools of resistance.

Ahead of the UN day celebrating the world’s Indigenous Peoples on 9 August, three young Indigenous leaders shared how they are using their voices – and their creativity – to reach millions of people.

Among them are dancer and entrepreneur Marciele Albuquerque, from the Munduruku people; singer-songwriter Kaê Guajajara, from the Guajajara people; and photographer and communicator Cristian Wariu, from the Xavante people.

All three are members of the UN’s Verified initiative, which works to counter climate-related misinformation.

© UNICEF/Paulo Diogenes

‘The forest no longer provides’

Marciele grew up in Juruti, in the Brazilian Amazon, where childhood meant swimming in rivers and gathering fruit steps from her village. Returning home today tells a different story.

“We can feel it’s getting hotter every year,” she said. “The fruits are no longer as abundant as they used to be. We once found them close to the village, right in the forest. Now we have to walk much farther, and even then there isn’t the same quantity. Droughts have become extreme, and so have the floods.”

Wildfires reshape the Cerrado

Cristian Wariu comes from the Parabubure Indigenous Territory in Mato Grosso state, where increasingly intense wildfires are transforming the Cerrado biome and disrupting daily life.

“Life has become increasingly unsustainable because these fires are now uncontrollable,” he said. “They severely affect the Xavante people’s food chain, and that also makes it easier for foods that are not good for our people to enter our communities. One problem leads to another, and eventually it reaches our health.”

The UN estimates more than 370 million Indigenous people worldwide are already experiencing the impacts of climate change, as global temperatures continue to rise.

Marcelo Camargo/Agência Brasil

Songs of displacement

Kaê Guajajara, born in Mirinzal in Maranhão state, believes today’s environmental crisis reflects a development model imposed on Indigenous peoples.

For her, distinguishing fact from misinformation is critical to helping vulnerable communities prepare for climate threats before they strike – and music has become an act of resistance in itself.

“Our traditional songs once celebrated the beauty of nature and our relationship with it,” she said. “Today, those same songs speak about our territories and about being forcibly removed from them. They tell the story of deforestation because we’re living it.”

SESC Santana/ @visaovh

Around half of Brazil’s Indigenous population now lives in cities, including Kaê, who was raised in Rio de Janeiro’s Maré favela. She is calling for stronger public policies to support Indigenous communities in urban settings, and sees a growing Indigenous presence in Brazil’s music industry as a chance to heal what she calls a long-standing colonial wound.

‘Visibility has become power’

Cristian credits earlier generations of Indigenous leaders with securing constitutional rights and building organizations that strengthened citizenship. His generation, he said, is fighting on a different front.

“Demarcation is no longer just about politics. It’s also about occupying screens. One strengthens the other,” he said. “When I look at the Indigenous movement as a whole, I believe our generation’s greatest contribution has been communication.”

Arquivo Pessoal / Cristian Wariu

Marciele Albuquerque understands that idea well. She is the first Indigenous woman ever chosen as Cunhã-Poranga – the highest female cultural title – at Brazil’s Parintins Folklore Festival, which she won this year performing with Boi Caprichoso. The victory song, Guerreira das Lutas (Warrior of the Struggles), names Indigenous peoples across Brazil, and still moves her each time she hears it.

“I’m not representing only my own people,” she said. “I’m representing Brazil’s extraordinary Indigenous diversity.” For her, “art is a way of fighting.”

Arquivo Pessoal / Marciele Albuquerque Munduruku

Kaê makes a similar case through music, rejecting the idea that Indigenous people lose their identity by using smartphones or making electronic music. “Today it’s increasingly common to hear the sound of the maracá alongside synthesizers,” she said.

Roots will push through

Her song Samaúma, named for a majestic, centuries-old tree revered by many Indigenous peoples, captures her philosophy: “No matter how much concrete you pour onto the ground, the roots will always push through. They will always grow and break the concrete, taking everything back.”

All three share the same conviction: rather than weakening their communities, the challenges ahead are making them stronger, more united, and determined to keep occupying new spaces.

articles.personality_title: Brazil’s Indigenous youth use culture and digital tools to protect their lands
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Indigenous peoples in Brazil are facing serious changes caused by climate change. Their forests are hotter, food is harder to find, and wildfires are damaging their lands. Many young Indigenous people are responding by sharing their stories and culture online.

**What happened** – Before the United Nations’ Indigenous Peoples Day on August 9, three young Indigenous leaders spoke about how they use music, dance, photography, and social media to raise awareness. Marciele Albuquerque, a dancer from the Munduruku people; Kaê Guajajara, a singer from the Guajajara people; and Cristian Wariu, a photographer from the Xavante people, all use their creativity to show what their communities face and fight against wrong information about climate change.

**Impact** – Their work is important because it helps more people understand the real effects of climate change on Indigenous lands. For example, Marciele talks about how fruits are disappearing near her village, and Cristian explains how wildfires harm their food and health. Kaê uses songs to tell stories about being forced from their lands. By sharing these stories online and through art, they keep their culture alive and build support.

**What's next step** – These young leaders will continue to use their voices and digital platforms to reach wider audiences. They hope this will lead to stronger laws and better support for Indigenous communities, especially in cities where many now live. Their efforts may inspire others to protect Indigenous rights and the environment.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Young Indigenous people in Brazil are combining culture and technology to protect their lands and share their stories with the world.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les jeunes autochtones du Brésil utilisent la culture et le numérique pour protéger leurs terres
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Les peuples autochtones du Brésil subissent de graves changements à cause du changement climatique. Les forêts deviennent plus chaudes, la nourriture se fait plus rare et les incendies détruisent leurs terres. Beaucoup de jeunes autochtones répondent en partageant leurs histoires et leur culture en ligne.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Avant la Journée des peuples autochtones des Nations Unies, le 9 août, trois jeunes leaders autochtones ont expliqué comment ils utilisent la musique, la danse, la photographie et les réseaux sociaux pour sensibiliser. Marciele Albuquerque, danseuse du peuple Munduruku ; Kaê Guajajara, chanteuse du peuple Guajajara ; et Cristian Wariu, photographe du peuple Xavante, utilisent leur créativité pour montrer les défis de leurs communautés et combattre les fausses informations sur le climat.

**Impact** – Leur travail est important car il aide à mieux comprendre les effets réels du changement climatique sur les terres autochtones. Par exemple, Marciele parle de la disparition des fruits près de son village, et Cristian explique comment les incendies affectent leur nourriture et leur santé. Kaê utilise des chansons pour raconter les histoires de déplacement. En partageant ces récits en ligne et par l’art, ils maintiennent leur culture vivante et créent du soutien.

**Prochaine étape** – Ces jeunes leaders continueront à utiliser leur voix et les plateformes numériques pour toucher un public plus large. Ils espèrent que cela mènera à des lois plus fortes et un meilleur soutien pour les communautés autochtones, surtout en ville où beaucoup vivent désormais. Leurs efforts pourraient inspirer d’autres à protéger les droits autochtones et l’environnement.

**En une phrase** – Les jeunes autochtones du Brésil allient culture et technologie pour protéger leurs terres et partager leurs histoires avec le monde.
articles.personality_title_es: Los jóvenes indígenas de Brasil usan la cultura y la tecnología para proteger sus tierras
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Los pueblos indígenas en Brasil enfrentan grandes cambios debido al cambio climático. Sus bosques son más calientes, la comida es más difícil de encontrar y los incendios dañan sus tierras. Muchos jóvenes indígenas están respondiendo compartiendo sus historias y cultura en línea.

**Qué pasó** – Antes del Día de los Pueblos Indígenas de la ONU el 9 de agosto, tres jóvenes líderes indígenas hablaron sobre cómo usan la música, la danza, la fotografía y las redes sociales para crear conciencia. Marciele Albuquerque, bailarina del pueblo Munduruku; Kaê Guajajara, cantante del pueblo Guajajara; y Cristian Wariu, fotógrafo del pueblo Xavante, usan su creatividad para mostrar lo que enfrentan sus comunidades y combatir la desinformación sobre el clima.

**Impacto** – Su trabajo es importante porque ayuda a que más personas entiendan los efectos reales del cambio climático en las tierras indígenas. Por ejemplo, Marciele cuenta cómo las frutas desaparecen cerca de su pueblo, y Cristian explica cómo los incendios afectan su comida y salud. Kaê usa canciones para contar historias sobre el desplazamiento. Al compartir estas historias en línea y a través del arte, mantienen viva su cultura y crean apoyo.

**Próximo paso** – Estos jóvenes líderes seguirán usando sus voces y plataformas digitales para llegar a más personas. Esperan que esto lleve a leyes más fuertes y mejor apoyo para las comunidades indígenas, especialmente en las ciudades donde muchos ahora viven. Sus esfuerzos pueden inspirar a otros a proteger los derechos indígenas y el medio ambiente.

**Una frase clave** – Los jóvenes indígenas de Brasil combinan cultura y tecnología para proteger sus tierras y compartir sus historias con el mundo.

articles.title: Can AI help build peace? African youth are showing a path forward
articles.summary: How are African youth using AI to build peace? What are some of the challenges that come with using AI for peace?
articles.content:
This article by Dan Campbell was originally published by Peace News Network on July 20, 2026. An edited version is being republished on Global Voices under a content partnership agreement.

How are African youth using Artificial intelligence (AI) to build peace? What are some of the challenges that come with using AI for peace?

Artificial intelligence often dominates headlines for its risks and misuses: Misinformation, surveillance, job losses, and deepfakes. Far less attention is paid to another story unfolding across Africa. Young people are using digital technologies to detect conflict early, counter hate speech, and strengthen community resilience.

A recent policy brief by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS Africa) argues that African youth are not simply adapting to AI. They are helping shape how digital technologies are used for peacebuilding. At the same time, the report warns that outdated policies, weak digital infrastructure, and persistent inequality threaten to limit that potential.

African governments, regional organizations, and civil society are beginning to develop AI governance frameworks that will influence how these technologies are used for years to come. One of the report’s central messages is that young people should not be consulted only after these frameworks are written. They should help design them from the beginning.

That argument deserves serious attention.

The report’s greatest strength is its refusal to portray African youth as passive recipients of technology. Instead, it presents them as knowledge creators who generate information, build digital tools, and shape public conversations about conflict. This is an important shift. Discussions of youth, peace, and security often focus on participation or representation. Here, the emphasis is on expertise. Young peacebuilders are producing the data, local knowledge, and digital innovations that increasingly underpin conflict prevention efforts.

The examples illustrate this well. Kenya’s Ushahidi platform demonstrated, following post-election violence from 2007 to 2008, how citizens could crowdsource reports during crises. More recent initiatives such as iVerify, piloted in Zambia in 2021, train young journalists to identify and counter false information before it spreads further. iVerify is now being used in Sierra Leone and Liberia as a Digital Public Good, where young journalists are being trained in fact-checking. Other youth-led projects combine machine learning, open-source intelligence, and community reporting to monitor elections, identify conflict risks, and challenge false narratives online.

Perhaps most importantly, the report avoids treating technology as a substitute for human relationships. Many of its strongest examples combine digital platforms with face-to-face dialogue, community organizing, local radio, and peace education. Digital tools become effective because they strengthen existing social networks rather than replace them.

The report is equally persuasive in highlighting barriers that continue to shape Africa’s digital future.

Internet access remains deeply unequal across the continent, especially in rural and conflict-affected areas. Women continue to face significant obstacles to digital participation. African languages remain poorly represented in many AI systems, limiting the ability of automated tools to understand local contexts or identify harmful content accurately. AI systems trained primarily in English or other Western languages risk failing to detect harmful content in African languages. These are not simply technical shortcomings. They are questions of inclusion, legitimacy, and whose voices are heard.

The discussion of language is especially important. Peacebuilding depends on understanding local narratives and community dynamics.

The recommendations are practical and well aligned with the evidence presented. They call for closer coordination between the African Union (AU)’s peace and technology institutions, greater investment in digital literacy and connectivity, stronger ethical oversight of AI, and formal mechanisms that allow young people to contribute directly to peace and security policymaking.

Even so, some questions remain unanswered.

The report presents a series of encouraging initiatives but offers relatively little evidence about their long-term impact. Which digital peacebuilding approaches have measurably reduced violence? Which have strengthened trust between communities? Which have struggled to move beyond successful pilot projects? As governments and donors invest more resources in AI for peacebuilding, these questions become increasingly important.

The paper also could have explored more fully the tension between AI’s promise and its potential misuse. Technologies developed for early warning or conflict monitoring may also expand state surveillance or restrict civic space if deployed without meaningful oversight. Strong governance frameworks become essential not simply because AI is powerful, but because power itself requires accountability.

These limitations, however, do not diminish the report’s broader contribution. Rather, they point toward the next generation of research that will be needed as digital peacebuilding matures across the continent.

At its heart, this policy brief offers a valuable reminder that peacebuilding is not only about technology. It is about people. AI may improve early warning systems, detect misinformation more quickly, or support better conflict analysis. Yet none of these advances will produce lasting peace unless they reflect local knowledge, community priorities, and public trust.

Across Africa, young people are already demonstrating what that future can look like. The challenge now is whether institutions will recognize them as equal partners in shaping it.

For policymakers, civil society organizations, and international partners, the message is clear: Investing in digital peacebuilding means investing in the people who understand their communities best. Africa’s AI future will be strongest not when technology replaces local leadership, but when it amplifies it.
articles.reasoning: The article highlights a positive real-world impact where African youth are actively using AI to build peace, counter hate speech, and strengthen community resilience, which has broad societal significance. It focuses on youth-led digital peacebuilding initiatives with detailed examples and discusses the importance of inclusive governance frameworks, thus providing substantial context. The story is inspiring as it portrays young people as knowledge creators shaping AI for peace, emphasizing empowerment and ethical use of technology for social good.
articles.personality_title: African youth use AI to build peace and fight hate speech
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Many people hear about how artificial intelligence (AI) can cause problems like fake news or job loss. But in Africa, young people are using AI in a different way: to help prevent conflicts, stop hate speech, and support their communities.

**What happened** – A recent report by the Institute for Security Studies (ISS Africa) shows that African youth are not just using AI but shaping how it helps build peace. Projects like Kenya’s Ushahidi platform gather crisis reports from citizens, and Zambia’s iVerify trains young journalists to spot false information. These tools combine technology with real conversations and community work to be more effective.

**Impact** – This approach is important because it treats young people as experts and creators, not just users. It helps communities catch problems early and build trust. The report also points out challenges like poor internet access, language barriers, and lack of fair rules, which can limit these efforts. Making sure AI understands local languages and involves young people in decision-making is key.

**What’s next step** – Governments and organizations need to work together to improve internet access, digital skills, and ethical rules for AI. They should include young people from the start when making laws about AI and peace. Researchers also want to learn which projects truly reduce violence and help communities the most.

**One-sentence takeaway** – African youth are leading the way in using AI to support peace by combining technology with local knowledge and community action.
articles.personality_title_fr: Les jeunes Africains utilisent l’IA pour construire la paix et lutter contre la haine
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Beaucoup de gens entendent parler des problèmes liés à l’intelligence artificielle (IA), comme les fausses informations ou la perte d’emplois. Mais en Afrique, les jeunes utilisent l’IA d’une autre manière : pour prévenir les conflits, stopper les discours de haine et soutenir leurs communautés.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Un rapport récent de l’Institut pour les études de sécurité (ISS Africa) montre que les jeunes Africains ne se contentent pas d’utiliser l’IA, ils influencent la façon dont elle aide à construire la paix. Des projets comme la plateforme Ushahidi au Kenya collectent des rapports de crise des citoyens, et iVerify en Zambie forme de jeunes journalistes à repérer les fausses informations. Ces outils combinent technologie et travail communautaire pour être plus efficaces.

**Impact** – Cette approche est importante car elle considère les jeunes comme des experts et des créateurs, pas seulement des utilisateurs. Elle aide les communautés à détecter les problèmes tôt et à renforcer la confiance. Le rapport souligne aussi des défis comme le mauvais accès à Internet, les barrières linguistiques et le manque de règles équitables qui peuvent limiter ces efforts. Il est essentiel que l’IA comprenne les langues locales et que les jeunes participent aux décisions.

**Prochaine étape** – Les gouvernements et organisations doivent collaborer pour améliorer l’accès à Internet, les compétences numériques et les règles éthiques pour l’IA. Ils doivent inclure les jeunes dès le début lors de la création des lois sur l’IA et la paix. Les chercheurs veulent aussi savoir quels projets réduisent vraiment la violence et aident le plus les communautés.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Les jeunes Africains montrent la voie en utilisant l’IA pour soutenir la paix en combinant technologie, savoir local et action communautaire.
articles.personality_title_es: Los jóvenes africanos usan la IA para construir paz y combatir el discurso de odio
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – Muchas personas conocen los problemas que puede causar la inteligencia artificial (IA), como noticias falsas o pérdida de empleos. Pero en África, los jóvenes usan la IA de otra manera: para prevenir conflictos, detener el discurso de odio y apoyar a sus comunidades.

**Qué sucedió** – Un informe reciente del Instituto de Estudios de Seguridad (ISS África) muestra que los jóvenes africanos no solo usan la IA, sino que están ayudando a moldear cómo esta tecnología apoya la construcción de la paz. Proyectos como la plataforma Ushahidi en Kenia recopilan reportes de crisis de los ciudadanos, y iVerify en Zambia entrena a jóvenes periodistas para identificar información falsa. Estas herramientas combinan tecnología con trabajo comunitario para ser más efectivas.

**Impacto** – Este enfoque es importante porque considera a los jóvenes como expertos y creadores, no solo usuarios. Ayuda a las comunidades a detectar problemas temprano y a fortalecer la confianza. El informe también señala desafíos como el acceso limitado a internet, barreras lingüísticas y falta de reglas justas, que pueden limitar estos esfuerzos. Es clave que la IA entienda los idiomas locales y que los jóvenes participen en la toma de decisiones.

**Próximo paso** – Los gobiernos y organizaciones deben trabajar juntos para mejorar el acceso a internet, las habilidades digitales y las reglas éticas para la IA. Deben incluir a los jóvenes desde el principio al crear leyes sobre IA y paz. Los investigadores también quieren saber qué proyectos realmente reducen la violencia y ayudan más a las comunidades.

**Resumen en una frase** – Los jóvenes africanos lideran el uso de la IA para apoyar la paz combinando tecnología con conocimiento local y acción comunitaria.
